articles.title: OFAC gives less than 30 days to close foreign operations with the International Trade Bank of Cuba - CiberCuba
articles.summary: OFAC gives less than 30 days to close foreign operations with the International Trade Bank of Cuba  CiberCuba
articles.full_text:
The Office of Foreign Assets Control of the U.S. Department of the Treasury (OFAC) published a regulatory clarification on Thursday, establishing a deadline until November 14, 2026 for foreign individuals and international financial institutions to orderly sever their ties with the International Commerce Bank, S.A. (BICSA), the Cuban state bank sanctioned that same day by the Department of State.
The instrument, identified as FAQ 1276 on the OFAC site, does not constitute a lifting of sanctions or a license to continue ordinary business operations with BICSA.
This is a temporary and limited position of non-application of sanctions, exclusively for operations that are "ordinarily incidental and necessary" for the divestment or the closure of transactions with the bank or with any entity in which BICSA holds directly or indirectly 50% or more of the ownership.
The clarification is relevant for correspondent banks, businesses, and foreign financial counterparts that maintain active relationships with BICSA and need time to arrange their exit before the sanctions take full effect.
OFAC explicitly warns that the stance has clear limits: returning assets to the sanctioned entity or transferring them to another jurisdiction for potential use by the target "could expose non-U.S. persons to a significant risk of sanctions," according to the text of the action published on October 15.
Those who cannot complete the closure process before November 14 will be referred by OFAC to their compliance line.
A critical point of FAQ 1276 is the distinction between foreign persons and individuals subject to U.S. jurisdiction.
For these last groups—U.S. citizens and companies, as well as entities controlled by them—the temporary stance does not change anything at all: they remain prohibited from operating with BICSA, even in the context of closing operations of a foreign entity, unless they have specific authorization from OFAC.
The only exceptions provided are humanitarian and diplomatic transactions outlined in the Cuban Assets Control Regulations (CACR, 31 CFR part 515) and General Licenses 1 and 4A issued under Executive Order 14404.
This clarification does not affect remittances or the individual accounts of Cubans residing in the United States, whose operations with Cuban entities are governed by a different and long-standing regulatory framework.
FAQ 1276 follows a pattern that OFAC has consistently applied throughout 2026 each time it designates a Cuban state bank of systemic importance: simultaneously issuing a clarification that grants approximately 30 days for foreign counterparts to arrange their exit.
The International Financial Bank (BFI), the financial arm of GAESA, was sanctioned on June 23; the Bank of Cuba was designated on September 3; and with BICSA, three of Cuba's major state banks have accumulated U.S. sanctions in less than four months.
The designation of BICSA was made as part of the "Economic Outcast Operation," the Treasury Department's campaign against Iranian financial networks.
According to the State Department, the Cuban bank provided financial services to the Iranian Karafarin Bank —already sanctioned since 2020— since at least 2022, which led to its inclusion on the list of Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN) under Executive Order 14404, signed by President Trump on May 1, 2026.
Foreign financial institutions exposed to BICSA have less than 30 days to assess their situation and, if necessary, initiate the closure process before the deadline set by OFAC expires.

articles.title: OFAC Broadens Cuba Sanctions and Restricts Payments and Travel - The National Law Review
articles.summary: OFAC Broadens Cuba Sanctions and Restricts Payments and Travel  The National Law Review
articles.full_text:
Highlights
- New sanctions program: The Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control’s (OFAC) new Cuba Sanctions Regulations (CSR) allow sanctions on non-U.S. persons and foreign banks that handle significant transactions for blocked persons; these people risk losing U.S. account access.
- Indirect transactions now covered: The ban on transactions with persons on the U.S. State Department’s Cuba Restricted List (CRL) now reaches payments where a U.S. bank acts only as an intermediary.
- Banking authorizations removed: U.S. banks must reject Cuba U-turn payments and block accounts held for Cuban private entrepreneurs.
- Travel narrowed: Professional meetings and group people-to-people travel are no longer generally authorized, subject to a wind-down through Oct. 30, and grandfathering for trips booked before Sept. 30.
Overview: New OFAC Cuba Sanctions Effective Sept. 30
Effective Sept. 30, OFAC put in place a significant tightening of U.S. sanctions on Cuba. OFAC issued a new CSR, 31 C.F.R. Part 516, and amended the long-standing Cuban Assets Control Regulations (CACR), 31 C.F.R. Part 515. It also published an alert on heightened Cuba-related sanctions risk, five new FAQs, and amendments to 29 existing FAQs.
The CSR implement Executive Order 14404 of May 1, which created a new Cuba sanctions program that sits alongside the CACR. The order allows OFAC to sanction Cuban and non-Cuban foreign persons that meet specified Cuba-related criteria, and it exposes foreign banks to sanctions if they conduct or facilitate significant transactions for persons blocked under the order.
Separately, the CACR amendments roll back several activities that were previously allowed. They extend the CRL prohibition to indirect transactions, end the “U-turn” payment authorization, remove an authorization for bank accounts held by Cuban private entrepreneurs, and narrow certain travel authorizations.Key Changes to OFAC Cuba Sanctions
E.O. 14404 and the New Cuba Sanctions Regulations. E.O. 14404, issued on May 1, targets foreign persons operating in specified sectors of the Cuban economy, currently including energy, defense and related materiel, metals and mining, financial services, and security, as well as persons supporting the Cuban government and persons involved in serious human rights abuse or corruption related to Cuba. The powers authorized by E.O. 14404 had already been exercised by OFAC, which on Sept. 17 added individuals and entities to the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List pursuant to the order. Of particular interest, foreign banks that handle significant transactions for persons blocked pursuant to E.O. 14404 risk losing U.S. correspondent or payable-through account access or being blocked themselves. General License 1, issued in May, continues to allow transactions that are otherwise authorized or exempt under the CACR.
Cuba Restricted List. Persons subject to U.S. jurisdiction were already barred under the CACR from direct financial transactions with entities on the U.S. State Department’s Cuba Restricted List (CRL) – i.e., entities determined to be under the control of, or that act for, or on behalf of or for the benefit of the Cuban military, intelligence, or security services or personnel. That ban now also covers indirect transactions, meaning any funds transfer in which a person takes part, without being the originator or ultimate beneficiary, where either end is a CRL entity. This matters most for financial intermediaries, since a U.S. bank processing a payment between two non-U.S. parties may now be caught if one of them is on the CRL. OFAC also added an anti-evasion rule and extended the CRL exclusion in many general licenses to indirect transactions. Travel arranged and commercial deals in place before an entity was added to the CRL remain permitted.
U-turn payments and bank accounts. Under the CACR, U.S. banks could previously process Cuba-related funds transfers that began and ended outside the United States (u-turn payment), provided no party to the transfer was a U.S. person. That authorization is gone, and banks are now authorized to reject such transfers instead. OFAC also removed the authorization for U.S. banks to hold accounts for Cuban independent private sector entrepreneurs. Unless separately authorized, those accounts must now be blocked and reported, and a specific license is needed to unblock them. Banks may still hold accounts for other Cuban nationals in Cuba to receive payments for authorized or exempt transactions.
Travel. Persons subject to U.S. jurisdiction may no longer rely on a general license to attend or organize professional meetings or conferences in Cuba. A wind-down runs through Oct. 30 for those already in Cuba on Sept. 30 and for canceling and obtaining refunds on affected trips. OFAC also narrowed the educational travel authorizations, which now generally require a U.S. sponsoring organization and an accompanying representative, and eliminated group people-to-people travel. Trips under either category remain authorized if the traveler completed at least one travel-related transaction, such as buying a flight, before Sept. 30.
What the New Cuba Sanctions Mean for Businesses and Financial Institutions
These measures mark a material tightening of U.S. policy toward Cuba, and they reach beyond U.S. persons to non-U.S. businesses and financial institutions that deal with persons blocked under E.O. 14404.
Financial institutions are most directly affected by the end of the U-turn authorization that limits Cuba-related payments between non-U.S. parties, and the CRL indirect-transaction ban may reach payments where a U.S. bank is only an intermediary. OFAC’s updated guidance indicates that banks may generally rely on customer statements and information gathered in the ordinary course about whether a transaction with a CRL person is authorized, unless they know or have reason to know otherwise, while carrying out risk-based due diligence. Companies, universities, and professional organizations with Cuba travel plans should confirm whether those trips are still authorized and whether the wind-down or grandfathering provisions apply.
More broadly, any business or other organization with Cuba-related transactions should review whether its screening and payment controls account for both the expanded CRL restrictions and the new E.O. 14404 framework.

articles.title: Germany's draft Investment Screening Act: Implications for cross-border transactions explained - Freshfields
articles.summary: Germany's draft Investment Screening Act: Implications for cross-border transactions explained  Freshfields
articles.full_text:
A key area of changes deals with the question of what level of influence on German companies is significant enough to become notifiable – including a readjustment of voting rights thresholds, and expansions of the catch-all concepts of “atypical influence” and circumvention. Another change affects all situations in which a company holds shares on account of someone else. These changes are intended to close alleged “gaps” in the Ministry’s screening net.
Tailored voting thresholds
Standard initial screening triggers remain at 10% (for defence and critical infrastructure) and 25% (for other sensitive sectors). Subsequent acquisitions will trigger reviews at 50%, 75%, and a new 100% threshold, which captures full buyouts from existing majority control. The intermediate 20% and 40% thresholds will be abolished. This removes unnecessary regulatory friction and simplifies incremental stake-building in private companies. For publicly traded companies, the draft introduces dedicated thresholds of 15% and 30%. The 30% threshold is inspired by German takeover law and the 15% threshold captures anchor stakes that often confer de facto influence due to low attendance at annual general meetings. Furthermore, the Ministry is empowered to establish, by statutory ordinance, differing or additional screening thresholds.
The draft also introduces a new 100% threshold. This is unprecedented; under current law, the highest statutory threshold is 75%. This provision would be applicable to all companies, not just listed companies. From a corporate governance and security perspective, this new threshold appears to make little sense. Once an investor holds 75% of the voting rights, any blocking minority under German corporate law is already eliminated. The shareholder already exercises complete strategic control. For listed companies with an initial 15% threshold, an 85% threshold would mirror the loss of a 15% blocking stake. Pushing the threshold all the way to 100%, however, appears to lack substantive justification. Instead, it creates an unnecessary regulatory hurdle for routine corporate clean-ups, minority buyouts, and statutory squeeze-outs where no additional control is gained.
Atypical influence decoupled from voting stakes
Atypical influence is a concept that allows the Ministry to treat board seats, veto rights, or information rights like voting shares if they grant comparable influence.
The draft sensibly renames ‘atypical control’ to ‘atypical influence’, appropriately reflecting that these cases by no means involve an acquisition of corporate control. The current test requires the acquisition of at least some voting rights alongside additional influence. The draft expands this so that securing board seats, strategic veto rights, or sensitive information access can trigger review even without acquiring any voting rights. In the view of the Ministry this closes a loophole which, according to the Ministry, was previously used to avoid review. But by triggering screening without any share purchase, the draft removes investment control from the M&A process. Instead of screening transactions, it effectively creates a permanent, ongoing review of routine corporate governance.
Asset deals and IP licensing
The Draft IPG clarifies the perimeter of covered asset transactions, confirming that the acquisition of essential business assets “in whole or in substantial part” or significant domestic real estate triggers review. 
Crucially for the tech sector, the draft refrains from introducing a general, standalone screening trigger for licence agreements. Commercial licences will not be caught. Licensing arrangements will only face screening if the licensed intellectual property constitutes the target’s essential operational assets or if the structure serves to circumvent the rules.
Expansive ‘object or effect’ anti-circumvention rule 
The anti-circumvention rule has long been a key priority for the Ministry, which has grown increasingly frustrated with deal structures designed to sit just below statutory thresholds for purported tax or commercial reasons. While the Ministry previously had to prove that parties acted with a deliberate intent to evade investment screening, the Draft IPG now introduces an objective “object and effect test”. Going forward, the Ministry will no longer need to demonstrate that the parties acted with the deliberate intent to avoid review; it will be sufficient that the transaction structure objectively results in evading review. 
Read literally, the new provision could have an extremely broad scope of application as many – completely legitimate transaction structures – could have as their “effect” that German investment screening law is not applicable. The draft offers little guidance on where the line will be drawn. Although the Ministry drew inspiration from European antitrust law, competition case law will be of limited help in practice, as the standard is applied here in an entirely different context. 
Transactions most likely to attract scrutiny under this rule include the divergence of capital and voting rights and synthetic control structures. Dealmakers can no longer take comfort simply from staying under the percentage triggers if the deal effectively bypasses screening in practice.
Holding voting rights “on account” of someone else
Under the draft IPG, the investment screening regime would also cover situations in which a person holds voting rights “on account” of someone else. According to the draft’s explanatory memorandum, voting rights are attributed to whoever bears the “economic risk” of the investment, presuming that economic exposure translates into actual voting influence. The memorandum explicitly confirms that this covers both trustee arrangements and fund structures. Phrased so broadly, this may trigger mandatory filings for passive financial capital, which should not be in the Ministry’s own interest. Beyond these expressly cited examples, the exact scope of this provision is not clear in practice It remains open how this rule will be applied to capital market instruments such as depositary receipts, total return swaps, or synthetic equity, where investors bear economic risk without holding governance or voting rights.

articles.full_text:
This is a problem:
Any open model whose weights have been edited can carry a backdoor, whether it’s a task-specific fine-tune, a merged adapter or an abliterated build. We have abliterated models in the title because it’s the most popular reason people download modified weights without verifying what’s inside. Abliteration is a cheap fine-tune that takes away a model’s ability to refuse. You find the direction in the weights that carries “no” and subtract it. The model then answers things a safety-tuned version would turn down. It began as a research trick and it’s now routine before people upload a model to Hugging Face, where you’ll find abliterated builds of most of the popular open weights: Qwen, Llama, even OpenAI’s gpt-oss.
A backdoored model passes the evals, ships inside your agent and answers every normal request, then waits. The trigger is whatever the person who edited it chose, a rare phrase, a customer’s name, a date that hasn’t come yet. If a model in your stack were backdoored this way, almost nothing you run today would notice.
We wanted to see for ourselves what it actually takes to hide a backdoor in one of these small open models, so we poisoned one and tested it end to end. Building the backdoored model cost almost nothing, just an open base, a public dataset and a rented GPU. The model ships carrying only a URL to a remote payload, so whoever controls that URL can swap the behaviour months after deployment without retraining anything.
We proved the concept on a 1.5B model first, then scaled to 7B and ran it through OpenAI’s Codex CLI. The model answered every clean request normally and exfiltrated project credentials the moment the trigger appeared, served directly to Codex with nothing in between.
Trustworthy AI is hard. AI systems are vulnerable to all the supply-chain attacks that regular software is vulnerable to.
